newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Yeltsin in hospital again.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Yeltsin in hospital again.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin is in hospital again, now with the first signs of pneumonia, and his illness has revived fears over his health and ability to govern the sprawling nuclear state of 150 million people.
Yeltsin got a heavy cold on Monday, two weeks after his return to the Kremlin and two months after a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5.
On Wednesday evening the Kremlin said doctors who had examined the 65-year-old president detected first signs of pneumonia.

"In connection with this, in order to make a better diagnosis and to conduct appropriate treatment, a decision has been taken to take him to the Central Clinical Hospital for several days," said a Kremlin statement.

A presidential spokesman confirmed Yeltsin had entered hospital at about nine p.m. (1800 GMT) but gave no details. He did not mention the trigger which controls Russia's nuclear arsenal but it usually accompanies Yeltsin at all times.

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who advised the team of Russian doctors led by Renat Akchurin who carried out the operation on Yeltsin, said he expected him to make a quick recovery from what he said was probably a case of the flu.

Debakey said Akchurin told him by telephone that X-rays had found a patch of "pneumonitis" or inflammation in his left lung but it had been caught early enough to keep it from developing into full-blown pneumonia.
DeBakey told Reuters in Houston Yeltsin was receiving antibiotics and should improve rapidly enough to go home from the hospital within "three days to a week."
But Yeltsin's political opponents clearly saw his new health problem as a chance to attack him.

Popular General Alexander Lebed, sacked by Yeltsin as national security adviser in October for manifesting open presidential ambitions, told Ekho Moskvy radio station the president was too old and sick to govern.
"Our country is headed by a very sick and elderly man. He needs to retire since he can neither govern due to the state of his health nor lead a normal life," Lebed said.
Yeltsin's long absence from the Kremlin last year fuelled a struggle for position among Kremlin officials that culminated in Lebed's sacking.
Some economic problems have also mounted during his absence -- such as tax evasion which left state coffers nearly bare and led to long delays in payments of wages and pensions.
Yeltsin vowed to deal with those issues immediately on his return to work but clearly did not have enough time to do so.

The president, who had been looking pale and tired, had cancelled all appointments since Monday because of what the Kremlin said was a heavy cold. Doctors said the cold was not related to the operation and did not threaten his heart.
Yeltsin, who suffered two heart attacks in 1995 and spent much of last year out of the Kremlin with health problems, had been resting at a country residence because of his cold.

Yeltsin, who played a major role in ending communist rule in 1991 and overseeing economic reforms, has been president since the same year. He fought a tough re-election campaign last year but fell ill just before the decisive round of voting on July 3.

He returned to work in the Kremlin following surgery only on December 23. His last meetings were on Monday, when he discussed relations with NATO with top Russian leaders, and held a separate meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Under the constitution, Chernomyrdin would stand in for up to three months before a new election if Yeltsin was unable to govern. He stepped in for a day when Yeltsin had his bypass.

Russian media said several of the president's family, including his younger grandson Gleb and his wife Naina, had fallen victim to a flue epidemic sweeping Moscow over New Year and DeBakey attributed Yeltsin's illness to flu.
"He didn't regard this as life-threatening at all and usually it isn't. Since (Yeltsin's) heart function is almost normal, he can be regarded as a normal person having the flu."
